transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Well, doc, to be honest, I'm... I'm not entirely sure where to begin, because if you looked at my life, you know, I manage large-scale engineering projects. I'm used to calling the shots, keeping everything on a strict timeline, managing dozens of contractors at once. I'm a guy who is always in the driver's seat. 

But lately—well, for a while now, actually—my evenings have just become this... this bizarre ordeal. I'll get home, and maybe I'm just trying to unwind after dealing with site plans all day, you know how it is, just trying to have a quiet night. But then, what brings me in is that once I start eating at night, it's like a switch flips and I completely lose the wheel. It's the strangest, most frustrating thing. It feels almost like... like I'm standing outside of my own body. I can actually see myself doing it, and in my head, I'm practically shouting, you know, telling myself to just stop, put the food down, walk away from the kitchen. I'm literally reasoning with myself, giving myself direct orders like I would to one of my foremen. 

But my hands... my hands just keep going back for more. It's like they have a mind of their own, completely bypassing my brain, just reaching and grabbing, and I can't seem to halt the process no matter how hard I tell myself to. It's just so unlike me. I mean, I'm a sixty-year-old man who oversees millions of dollars in structural developments, and I can't even stop my own hand from reaching into the pantry. It's just exhausting, frankly, and I realized I just can't seem to get a grip on it myself, no matter how many times I swear I'm going to.
Can you describe exactly what happens when you start eating at night? Do you feel like you're unable to stop eating once you start, or that you're eating much more rapidly than normal?

Well, it's... it's a whole process, really. I mean, I'll get home, right? Usually around 6:30 or 7:00, depending on traffic from the site. I'll take off my boots, wash up, and I'll think, 'Okay, let's just have a sensible dinner.' So, some evenings I'll start with just leftovers. Maybe some chicken and rice from the night before, you know, just a regular portion. I'll heat it up in the microwave, sit down at the island in the kitchen, and eat it. 

But then, before I even put the plate in the dishwasher, it starts. It's like the chicken and rice just... wasn't enough, or it didn't hit the spot, or something. So I'll think, 'Okay, maybe just a sandwich.' I'll make a turkey sandwich, maybe two. And I eat those. And I'm eating them fast, too, like I'm on a 15-minute lunch break at a site and trying to get back to work. 

Then, the sandwich is gone, and I'm still just... going. I'll move on to cereal. I'll pour a huge mixing bowl full of whatever cereal I have, eat that. Then I'm in the pantry, and I'm just grabbing cookies, chips, whatever snack food is in there. I'll eat half a sleeve of cookies, then a bag of pretzels. It just keeps escalating. I end up eating... I mean, it's far, far more than I would ever put on a plate for a normal supper. If you laid it all out on the counter before I started, it would look like I was feeding a whole crew of guys, not just myself. And the whole time, I'm just eating so rapidly, barely even tasting it, just... consuming it. It's like I can't stop the momentum once it starts.
When you start eating at night, do you feel like you can't stop eating, even if you want to?

Well, yeah, exactly. That's... that's really the crux of the whole issue, and honestly, it's what finally pushed me to make this appointment. I mean, I'm a logical guy, right? I spend my days analyzing blueprints, identifying structural flaws, anticipating problems before they happen. So, you'd think I could just apply that same logic to myself. 

But when I'm standing there in the kitchen, like I was saying before, it's like my brain and my body are completely disconnected. It's the most bizarre sensation. I'll be halfway through a box of cookies, and in my head, the rational part of me—the part that manages million-dollar budgets—is screaming, "What are you doing? You're not even hungry anymore! Put the box down and walk away!" I can literally hear my own internal monologue giving me a direct order to cease operations. 

But it's like... it's like my hands are deaf to it. They just keep moving. I reach into the box, pull out another cookie, shove it in my mouth, chew, swallow, repeat. And I'm watching myself do it. It's like I'm hovering a few feet away, observing this sixty-year-old man completely lose his mind over some baked goods. I want to stop, I really, genuinely do. I know it's ridiculous, I know I'm going to feel terrible physically and mentally afterward, but the brakes just don't work. The momentum is too strong, and I just... I can't seem to override whatever mechanism is making my hands keep reaching for more food. It's a complete and total loss of control, and frankly, it scares the hell out of me.
Do these nighttime eating episodes cause you significant distress, or interfere with your daily life in any way?

Well, distress? Absolutely. It’s... it’s a heavy thing to carry around. As for interfering with my life, it’s a bit complicated. I mean, on paper, I’m still functioning. I’m still getting up at 5:00 AM, still making it to the site, still managing my crews, still hitting my deadlines. The job gets done because, well, the job has to get done. I’ve never been one to let the ball drop professionally. 

But outside of work? That’s where the cracks are really starting to show. It’s... it’s embarrassing, honestly. I used to be a pretty active guy socially. I’ve got a group I’ve known for years, and we used to do things. We had this walking club, right? A bunch of us guys would get together on the weekends, walk a few miles, grab a coffee, talk about the market or sports or whatever. And my wife and I used to have a subscription to the local theater, we’d go to shows a couple of times a month. 

But lately... I’ve just been turning all of that down. I’ll make up excuses. I’ll say I’m too tired from the site, or I’ve got paperwork to catch up on, or my knee is acting up. But the truth is, I’m just... I’m so ashamed. I feel like this massive fraud. Here I am, this guy who is supposed to be in charge, who is supposed to have this iron-clad discipline, and I can’t even control what I put in my mouth at 8:00 PM. I’m constantly preoccupied with it. I worry about what people see when they look at me. Do they see the guy who manages million-dollar builds, or do they see a guy who lacks basic self-control? I feel like if I go out, if I’m around people, they’re going to somehow know. They’re going to look at me and think, 'He doesn't look disciplined.' It sounds ridiculous saying it out loud, but it just eats at me. So, yeah, I’m still working, but my actual life... the things I used to enjoy... I’m just isolating myself because I can’t stand the thought of people judging me for this... this weakness.
Do you find yourself eating alone during these nighttime episodes because you're embarrassed about how much you're eating?

Well, no, not exactly. I mean, I'm not sneaking off to the basement or locking myself in a room to eat, if that's what you're asking. My wife, she's usually right there in the house with me. 

We have this open-concept layout on the first floor. I actually oversaw the renovation myself a few years back—we knocked down the main load-bearing wall between the kitchen and the living room, put in a massive steel beam to open the whole space up. It flows really well now. Anyway, because of that layout, she’s usually just sitting right there on the sofa in the living room, watching her evening programs. She really likes those British mysteries, you know, the ones where everyone lives in some quaint little village but there's a murder every single week? She gets completely engrossed in them. 

And I'll be right there at the kitchen island, maybe twenty feet away. So I'm not alone, and I'm not hiding the fact that I'm eating. She sees me going back and forth to the pantry. I think she just assumes I had a really grueling day at the site and worked up a massive appetite, or maybe she just isn't paying that close attention because of her shows. But I definitely don't wait for her to go to bed or purposefully isolate myself to do it. I just... I eat right there in the open. It's not like I'm trying to be secretive about the actual physical act of eating, even though, like I said before, the whole thing makes me feel completely ashamed of myself. I just don't hide in the dark to do it.
Do you find yourself eating until you feel uncomfortably full during these nighttime eating episodes?

Well, uncomfortably full? No, I wouldn't say that. I mean, I know what you're getting at, that feeling like you've just eaten Thanksgiving dinner and you have to unbutton your pants and lay on the couch for three hours. But it's not really like that for me. 

Don't get me wrong, I eat a lot during these... these episodes, as you called them. Like I mentioned with the cookies, it's a significant amount of food. But my stomach doesn't usually get to that point of physical pain or stretching where I feel like I'm going to burst. I've always had a pretty cast-iron stomach, to be honest. Even back when I was a young guy working my way up on the framing crews, eating whatever garbage I could grab from the food trucks on a fifteen-minute break, I never really got stomach aches. 

So, yeah, I'm definitely eating way past the point of just being satisfied, and mentally, like I said, I feel absolutely sick about it. I feel heavy with the guilt of it all. But physically? My stomach itself doesn't usually hurt. I don't get that bloated, painful sensation where I'm physically uncomfortable from the sheer volume of it. It's more of a... a mental discomfort, I suppose you could say. The physical feeling of fullness is there, sure, but it doesn't cross over into actual physical pain or extreme discomfort. It's just... it's the lack of control that's the uncomfortable part, not my actual stomach.
Do you feel intense guilt, self-disgust, or emotional pain specifically during or after these nighttime eating episodes?

Guilt? Oh, absolutely. It’s… it’s overwhelming, to be honest. The guilt and the self-disgust, it just washes over me. It’s funny you ask if it’s during or after, because it’s really both, but they feel different. 

During the eating, it’s this strange mix of… I don't know, almost like a frantic energy, but underneath it, there’s this voice just screaming at me. I’ll be standing there at the island—like I said, with the open layout and my wife right there on the couch—and I’ll be reaching for another handful of whatever it is, and I’m thinking, "Why are you doing this? You don't need this. You're a grown man, for God's sake." But I just keep doing it. It’s like watching a train wreck, and I’m the conductor, but I can’t hit the brakes. The disgust starts building right then. I look at my hands, I look at the food, and I just feel this deep, profound disappointment in myself. 

And then… then after. Once I finally stop. That’s when the real emotional pain hits. It’s like a physical weight pressing down on my chest. I’ll look at the empty wrappers or the dent I put in the pantry, and I just feel sick to my stomach—not physically, like we talked about, but mentally. I feel like a complete failure. I’ve spent my whole life building things, right? Managing crews, making sure everything is plumb and level and exactly to spec. I pride myself on discipline. If a subcontractor is slacking, I’m the first one to pull them aside and read them the riot act. But here I am, unable to manage myself. 

I’ll just stand there in the kitchen, and this wave of shame just completely engulfs me. I think about what my crew would say if they saw me. I think about what my wife would think if she really paid attention and saw the sheer volume of what I’m putting away. It’s just… it’s a terrible, terrible feeling. It makes me feel weak. And in my line of work, in my life, weakness isn't something I tolerate well, especially not in myself. So, yeah, the guilt and the disgust… they’re probably the hardest parts of this whole thing. It just eats away at whatever self-respect I have left.
During these nighttime eating episodes, do you feel like you have absolutely no choice but to keep eating, like it's an urge or compulsion you can't resist, even though you know you should stop?

Yeah... yeah, that's exactly it. Compulsion, urge, whatever you want to call it. It’s actually the whole reason I finally picked up the phone and made the appointment to see you. 

What brings me in is that once I start eating at night, it feels like I can literally see myself doing it and telling myself to stop, but my hands just keep going back for more. It’s the most bizarre, frustrating thing in the world. Because, you have to understand, my whole life, my entire career, is built on control and precision. If a concrete pour is going sideways on a site, I step in, I blow the whistle, I tell the crew to stop, and everything stops. My brain gives the command, and the action follows. 

But standing there at that kitchen island... it's like the wiring between my brain and my body is completely severed. I’m standing there, looking at the food, and in my head, I am yelling at myself. I'm saying, "Put the package down. Walk away. You don't want this." I am actively, consciously telling myself to stop. But it's like I'm just a passenger in my own body watching a movie of someone else. My hands just keep going back into the pantry, reaching into the box, bringing it to my mouth, over and over again. 

I've worked with my hands my entire life, right? From framing houses back in the day to drafting blueprints, my hands have always done exactly what I told them to do, down to the fraction of an inch. So to stand in my own house, with my wife twenty feet away watching her shows, and just watch my own hands keep grabbing food while my brain is screaming to shut the whole operation down... it's terrifying, frankly. It really is. I just completely lose the ability to steer the ship. That's why I'm sitting here talking to you today. Because I can't manage my own two hands once that switch flips, and I just can't live with that feeling of having absolutely zero choice in the matter.

Can you recall if this urge to keep eating at night feels different from regular hunger — like it's an intense, irresistible need that you absolutely have to act on, even if you know it doesn't make sense?

A need? I... I'm not really sure I'd use that word. I don't know if I've ever noticed it feeling like a *need*, exactly. 

I mean, regular hunger, sure, I know exactly what that feels like. You spend thirty-five years in the construction business, you learn what real, physical hunger is. You're out there on a site in the middle of July, sun beating down on the back of your neck, you've been on your feet since five in the morning, hauling materials, checking grades, arguing with the suppliers... by the time noon rolls around, your stomach is completely hollow. You *need* fuel. Your body is physically demanding calories just to keep the engine running so you don't pass out on the scaffolding. That's a need. You eat because if you don't, you can't work.

But this thing at night? I don't feel hungry. Not in that way. And I don't really feel an intense *need* to eat the food, either. It's not like my brain is screaming at me that I absolutely have to have a sleeve of crackers or a row of cookies. I'm not craving it. I don't have this irresistible desire welling up inside me where I feel like I have to act on it because I just *have* to taste the food or satisfy some deep urge. 

Honestly, I don't really know what to tell you on that front, because I just haven't noticed any kind of 'need' driving the whole operation. Like I was saying a minute ago, it's more of a mechanical failure. I'm just standing there, and my hands are doing the work, but there's no craving or intense emotional need pushing me to do it. It's not a need I'm trying to satisfy. If anything, I'm actively *not* wanting it while it's happening. 

So, no, I can't really say it feels like an irresistible need... I'm not entirely sure what you mean by that, to be honest. I don't feel a drive to do it, I just... do it. Without needing to. Does that make any sense? Because I'll tell you, it doesn't make a lick of sense to me. I just don't feel that specific 'need' you're talking about at all.
During these nighttime eating episodes, do you ever feel like your actions are automatic, as if you're on autopilot and not fully in control of your body?

Autopilot is exactly the word for it. Honestly, like I was telling you a few minutes ago, that specific feeling is exactly what brings me in here to see you. Once I start eating at night, it feels like I can literally see myself doing it, and I am standing there in my own kitchen telling myself to stop, but my hands just keep going back for more. It is completely automatic. 

You know, it’s kind of like... well, if you've ever driven the exact same route to a job site every single morning for six months straight. You leave the house at 4:30 AM, you get on the highway, you take the exit, and suddenly you're pulling your truck into the dirt lot and you don't even remember making the last four turns. Your brain just checked out, but your body did the driving. It’s like that, but honestly, it’s worse. Because when you're driving on autopilot, you're just spacing out. But with this... with the food... I am fully awake. I am completely aware. 

I’m standing there at the island, the television is murmuring in the living room—usually my wife is watching one of those home renovation shows, which, don't even get me started on how fake those are, the timelines they show are an absolute joke—and I'm just... operating. Like a piece of heavy machinery that got switched on, but the kill switch is busted. I'm looking at my own hand reaching into the pantry, grabbing whatever it is, bringing it up, chewing, swallowing, and then reaching right back in again. 

My brain is screaming, "Abort, shut it down, we're done here," but the body is just running its own program. I'm totally disconnected from it. So yes, autopilot is exactly it. You're just a passenger. And I've got to tell you, it's the most powerless, frustrating feeling in the world for a guy who has spent his entire adult life being the one in charge, the one steering the ship, making sure everyone else is doing exactly what they're supposed to do. To have my own body just go rogue on me like that... it’s completely out of my hands. Literally.
During these nighttime eating episodes, do you ever feel detached from yourself, like you're not fully present or you're watching yourself act from outside your body?

Yeah, exactly. I mean, it's like I've been trying to explain to you this whole time, right? That specific feeling is the exact reason I'm sitting in this chair today. Like I said, what brings me in is that once I start eating at night, it feels like I can literally see myself doing it and telling myself to stop, but my hands just keep going back for more. 

When you say "watching yourself act from outside your body," that hits the nail right on the head. It's... well, let me put it this way. You know when you're looking at a set of blueprints, and you're looking down at the whole floor plan from above? You can see where the load-bearing walls are, where the HVAC runs, the whole layout. You have this bird's-eye view of the entire operation. That's exactly what it feels like in my kitchen. 

I'm standing there by the kitchen island—we just put that granite in two years ago, beautiful stone, absolute nightmare of a subcontractor though, I had to stay on him every single second to make sure the seams lined up right—anyway, I'm standing there at the island, but it's almost like my mind is hovering up near the crown molding, just looking down at this sixty-year-old guy shoving food into his mouth. 

I am totally detached. I'm up there, so to speak, shouting down at myself, going, "Hey! Cut it out! Stop reaching into the cabinet! Put it away!" But the guy down there—which is me—just keeps doing it. It's the strangest, most unsettling thing. I'm present enough to know it's happening, and I'm actively trying to call off the job, but I'm completely disconnected from the physical act itself. Like my brain and my body are on two completely different job sites. 

So, yeah, detached is a very good word for it. It's just... it's exactly what I was saying before. I see myself doing it, I tell myself to stop, and I just can't. The hands just keep moving, completely on their own, while I just have to stand there and watch it happen from the outside. It's infuriating, doc, it really is. You spend your whole life building things, controlling every little detail on a massive project, and then you can't even control your own hands in your own house.
Can you confirm that these episodes of uncontrollable eating only happen in the evening or during the night, and not during other parts of the day?

Well, confirm? I don't know if I can confirm that, doc. I really couldn't say for sure if it's strictly a nighttime operation. I'm honestly not entirely sure. 

You see, in my line of work, the whole concept of 'day' and 'night' gets pretty blurry anyway. You've got jobs where we have to pour concrete at three in the morning because the city won't let us shut down the street during normal traffic hours. Or you're stuck in the site trailer at two in the afternoon on a Tuesday, fighting with the city inspectors over some permit issue that should have been resolved three weeks ago, and you end up working straight through dinner. My schedule is just a complete moving target, always has been. Thirty-five years of it, and you never really get a standard nine-to-five. You're just constantly putting out fires whenever they pop up.

Because my days are so all over the map like that, my eating habits are kind of all over the map, too. I might be grabbing a quick sandwich from a roach coach at ten in the morning, or I might eat absolutely nothing at all until I finally drag myself through the front door at seven. So if you're asking me to swear on a stack of blueprints that this... this autopilot thing, this loss of steering, *only* ever happens in the evening or at night? I just don't know. 

I haven't really kept a punch list of the exact times it happens. It definitely stands out to me at night, like I was saying before about being in the kitchen with the TV murmuring in the background and the wife watching her shows, because the house is quiet and I'm supposed to be winding down. But as for the rest of the day? I really haven't noticed if it's exclusive to the PM hours. I might have done it at three in the afternoon on a Sunday for all I know. I just haven't tracked it that closely to give you a solid yes or no on whether it's only happening after dark.
Do you ever experience this same feeling of being detached from yourself or watching yourself from outside your body at times other than these nighttime eating episodes?

Detached at other times? No, I... I really don't think so. Honestly, doc, my whole life, my entire day-to-day existence, is the exact opposite of that. I mean, you have to understand, in my line of work, you can't afford to be floating outside your body. You just can't. 

When you're managing a massive project, say, a fifty-unit commercial build, and you've got excavators moving around, cranes lifting steel beams, forty different guys who all need you to answer a question right this second... you have to be completely dialed in. I am the guy with boots on the ground. I feel the mud, I feel the ache in my knees from walking on concrete all day, I am one hundred percent present. If I spaced out or detached on a job site, somebody could get seriously hurt, or we'd pour a foundation wrong and cost the client hundreds of thousands of dollars. 

So, no, that whole... bird's-eye view thing I was telling you about? Looking down from the ceiling? That is strictly happening when I'm standing there with the pantry door swung open or my head in the fridge. The rest of the time, I am fully in the driver's seat. I deal in dirt and steel and concrete, you know? Real, tangible things. I'm a very grounded guy. 

That's probably why this whole thing is driving me so crazy. To go from being that locked in, calling all the shots and being totally engaged with the physical world all day, to suddenly feeling like a ghost watching some stranger eat in my own kitchen... it’s just bizarre. It goes against everything I am. But no, to answer your question, I haven't noticed that disconnected feeling anywhere else in my life. Just with the food.
Do you find yourself feeling detached, emotionally numb, or overwhelmed by negative emotions during times other than these nighttime eating episodes?

Well, like I was just saying about the detachment... no, not really. And as for being emotionally numb or overwhelmed by negative emotions? I really don't think so. 

I mean, don't get me wrong, doc, I get stressed. It's a high-stress job. You try coordinating a massive foundation pour when the weather forecast suddenly decides to dump two inches of rain on you, or you're dealing with an electrician who apparently can't read a basic schematic to save his life and wants to run wire right through a load-bearing beam. You get mad, sure. You get frustrated. I'll be the first to admit I can yell with the best of them when a sub is trying to cut corners. My blood pressure probably spikes, and I definitely bring some of that aggravation home with me. 

But overwhelmed by it? Or numb? No, no, no. You can't be numb in this business. If you go numb, the whole project falls apart. You have to be loud, you have to be completely present, you have to push through it and find a solution. I've been doing this for thirty-five years. I started right out of high school swinging a hammer, framing houses in the dead of winter, and worked my way up to managing these massive commercial sites. You don't survive in this industry by getting overwhelmed and shutting down. You just... you fix the problem. You adjust the schedule, you fire the guy who isn't pulling his weight, you just get it done. 

So no, I don't have any of that numb feeling or whatever you want to call it during my regular day-to-day. I don't sit around feeling sorry for myself or getting swallowed up by bad feelings. It's really just... it's exactly like I said, it's just this thing with the food. That's the one and only time I feel like I'm losing my grip or checking out. The rest of the time, I'm the guy holding the whole operation together. I have to be.
Do you ever find yourself not remembering these nighttime eating episodes afterward, or do you always remember exactly what happened while you were eating?

Well, remember it... yeah, I remember it. I wish I didn't, to be honest with you, but I do. It's not like a blackout or anything like that. I'm not waking up the next morning finding empty wrappers in the trash and wondering how they got there, like some kind of amnesia. No, I remember exactly what happened. 

I can tell you exactly what I pulled out of the fridge, what order I ate it in, how much of it there was. I remember the cold air from the freezer when I was digging out a pint of ice cream, and I remember exactly how I felt right after—that heavy, awful feeling in my gut. I remember all of it. It's just that *while* it's happening, like I said, it feels like I'm not the one driving the truck. But the memory of it? Oh, it's crystal clear. 

It's actually kind of the worst part, having to remember it all so vividly the next day. You're sitting there on a job site, trying to review a set of schematics with the foreman, and in the back of your head, you're just replaying the fact that you stood in the kitchen at midnight and ate an entire loaf of bread and half a jar of peanut butter, and you couldn't stop yourself. It's humiliating, frankly. So, yeah, I remember it. I remember every single detail. I just wish I could forget it, or better yet, just not do it in the first place. But no, no memory loss here. I know exactly what I did.
Do these nighttime eating episodes typically begin after you've already gone to bed and woken up during the night, or do they happen while you're still awake and active in the evening?

Well, it's... it's a mix, I guess you could say. It's not always the exact same routine. Sometimes it's right after dinner, you know? I'll get home from a site—usually late, maybe around seven or eight—and I'll eat a regular meal. A steak, some potatoes, whatever my wife made. And then I'll sit down in the recliner to watch the game or catch up on some emails, and... I don't know, I just never really settle. I'm still awake, still in my work clothes sometimes, and that urge just hits me. I'll wander back into the kitchen, and before I know it, I'm just eating everything in sight. 

But then there are other times... and these are the ones that really mess with my head, doc. I'll actually go to bed. I'll be dead tired, right? I mean, when you've been walking a site for ten hours, your body is just done. So I'll go to sleep, maybe around ten-thirty or eleven. And then... boom. I'm awake. It's like two in the morning, the house is completely pitch black, silent. My wife is sound asleep next to me. And my eyes just snap open, and I know exactly what I'm going to do. 

I don't even really think about it. I just throw the covers off, put my feet on the floor, and I'm walking down the hall to the kitchen. It's almost like a trance, even though I'm fully awake and I know exactly what's happening. I'll stand there in the dark, just the light from the refrigerator shining on me, and I'll eat cold leftovers, half a pie, cheese right off the block. 

So, it's both. Sometimes I haven't even made it to bed yet, and I'm just pacing around the house in the evening, and it happens. Other times, I've been asleep for hours, and something just wakes me up with this... this overwhelming drive to go eat. It's frustrating because I can't even predict it. If I knew it only happened when I was up late, maybe I'd just force myself to go to bed earlier, right? But since it happens when I wake up in the middle of the night too, I feel like I can't escape it. I'm either fighting it while I'm trying to relax in the evening, or it's pulling me out of a dead sleep. It's exhausting, honestly. Just exhausting.

Have you ever experienced episodes where you feel detached from yourself or your surroundings outside of these nighttime eating episodes, such as during times of stress or at random moments during the day?

Doc, I feel like we're covering the same ground here a bit. Like I was saying just a few minutes ago when you asked about the numbness... no. No detachment. Not during the day, not when I'm stressed, not at random. 

I really don't get detached. I don't float outside my body or lose touch with what's going on around me. If I did that on a job site, somebody could get killed, plain and simple. Just last Thursday, we had a crane operator swinging three tons of steel I-beams over a live deck to set the upper framing. You think I can afford to just... zone out? Feel detached from my surroundings? Hell no. My eyes are glued to the rig, my radio is tight in my hand, I'm checking the wind speed, I'm watching the guys on the ground tying off. You have to be dialed in. One hundred percent dialed in, every second. 

And even if I'm not out in the dirt, say I'm just sitting in the job trailer doing paperwork, going over fifty pages of change orders or arguing on the phone with a city inspector about some obscure fire code requirement they suddenly decided to enforce... I am fully there. I get stressed, sure. My neck gets tight, I might chew on a pen or snap at one of my supers because we're two weeks behind schedule and bleeding money, but I am entirely in my own skin. There are no random moments of just... drifting off into the ether. 

It's really just that food thing. Like I keep saying, that's the anomaly. That's the one time the steering wheel just spins in my hands. The rest of the day, for the other twenty-something hours, I am anchored to the ground. I'm sharp, I'm present, I'm handling the problems. I have to be, or sixty guys don't get paid and a multi-million dollar building doesn't go up. So no, absolutely no detachment outside of me standing in front of the fridge.
